summary: The west bank was Thebes' city of the dead: hidden royal tombs, temples for dead kings, nobles' tombs and the village of the men who built them.
look: Face west from the road coming off the river: first green fields, then a line of ruined temples along the edge of the farmland, then bare limestone hills full of tomb doorways. The pointed peak on the skyline is the Qurn. The Valley of the Kings hides behind the cliffs north of it, Deir el-Bahari sits at the foot of those cliffs on the near side, and Deir el-Medina and the Valley of the Queens lie further south.
story:
Egyptians lived on the east bank, where the sun rises, and buried their dead in the west, where it sets. Across the river from Karnak and Luxor Temple, Thebes kept a second city with its own priests, embalmers, police and craftsmen, all working for the dead. UNESCO lists the whole thing as 'Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis'.

The layout follows one big decision. From about 1539 BC the New Kingdom pharaohs gave up pyramids, which had all been robbed, and cut their tombs in a hidden desert valley behind the cliffs, under a peak shaped like a natural pyramid. Their temples moved away from the tombs to the edge of the fields, facing Thebes. The Egyptians called them 'mansions of millions of years': places where priests kept a dead king's cult alive every day. From north to south you can still trace them: Seti I at Qurna, Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari, the Ramesseum, Amenhotep III behind the Colossi of Memnon, and Ramesses III at Medinet Habu.

Between the temples and the valley, officials cut decorated tombs into the hills at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna and its neighbours, full of banquets and harvests. The workmen who dug and painted the royal tombs lived in a walled village at Deir el-Medina and walked to work over the hill.

The practical logic: each site has its own ticket. The standard Valley of the Kings ticket covers three tombs; Tutankhamun, Seti I and Ramesses V and VI each need an extra one, and Nefertari's tomb in the Valley of the Queens has its own, pricier ticket. Prices and rules change, so check at the window. Start early, carry more water than seems sensible, wear a hat, and never use flash.
details: The Qurn: the pyramid-shaped peak on the western skyline. Every royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings lies beneath it.
The Colossi of Memnon by the road: all that stands of Amenhotep III's temple, once the largest on this bank.
Dark square doorways in the hillside at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna: the Tombs of the Nobles.
Hatshepsut's terraced temple: a pale stripe of colonnades against the cliff below the Qurn, visible from the road.
fun_fact: The ancient Egyptians called the dead 'the westerners', so a funeral here really was a trip to the other side.
narration: You are on the west bank of Thebes, the side where the sun dies every evening, and so the side of the dead. The living city and the great temples of the gods were across the river, at Karnak and Luxor. Over here the kings built a second city: tombs, temples and workshops for eternity. Look west and read it like a map. First the green fields. Then, along the edge of the farmland, the big mortuary temples, which the Egyptians called mansions of millions of years, where priests fed a dead king's spirit every day. Then the bare limestone hills, pierced by hundreds of doorways: the tombs of officials. Behind the ridge, out of sight, is the Valley of the Kings, where the pharaohs hid their tombs after the age of pyramids. Above it all rises the Qurn, a peak shaped like a natural pyramid, probably one reason they chose the place. The men who cut and painted the royal tombs lived in their own walled village, Deir el-Medina, tucked into the hills to the south. A practical word. Every site has its own ticket. The standard Valley ticket covers three tombs, while Tutankhamun, Seti the First and Ramesses the Sixth cost extra. Carry more water than you think you need, and never use flash. Now find the pointed peak on the skyline: that is the Qurn, your compass for the whole day.

summary: For nearly 500 years Egypt's kings were buried here in hidden, painted tombs instead of pyramids; 65 are numbered, a handful open on any day.
look: You are in the main, or East, Valley: a dry limestone gully with tomb doors cut into its sides, each with a sign giving its KV number, plan and decoration. The visitor centre at the gate has a model of the valley, and a small electric tram runs up to the tombs. The pyramid-shaped peak of the Qurn rises to the south.
story:
Thutmose I's architect Ineni boasted in his own tomb that he dug the king's tomb with 'no one seeing, no one hearing'. That was the point. Every pyramid had been robbed, so from about 1539 BC the kings hid their tombs in this remote valley, guarded by the Medjay police, and built their temples far away by the fields. The Qurn probably helped: a natural pyramid over every grave. Burials went on until about 1075 BC, from Thutmose I to Ramesses X or XI.

There are 65 numbered tombs and pits, but only about twenty held kings. John Gardner Wilkinson painted the first numbers on 21 tombs in 1827. The plan evolved: early tombs turn at a right angle, Horemheb's jogs sideways, and Ramesside tombs run straight into the hill like long pipes, which is what Greek visitors called them: syringes. The walls carry the guidebooks of the afterlife: the Amduat, the Books of Gates, Caverns and the Earth, the Litany of Ra. All tell one story: the sun dies at dusk, crosses the twelve hours of the underworld and is reborn at dawn, with the king on board.

About 18 tombs can be opened, rarely all at once, so check the board at the gate. Worth the extra tickets: Ramesses V and VI (KV9) for the sky ceilings, Seti I (KV17) for sheer quality. On the standard ticket: Ramesses IV (KV2), Merenptah (KV8), Ramesses III (KV11), Tausert and Setnakht (KV14), Ramesses IX (KV6) and, knees permitting, Thutmose III (KV34). Tutankhamun's tomb is small; you saw the treasure on the 11th.

The valley gets 4,000 to 5,000 visitors on most days, so go early. Guides may not lecture inside tombs. Ancient tourists left over 2,100 Greek and Latin graffiti, the earliest dated 278 BC.
details: The sign at each tomb door: plan, date and decoration, designed by the Theban Mapping Project in 2001.
The model of the valley in the visitor centre: see how the tombs dive into the hills and pass close to each other.
From the valley floor, look up at the Qurn: 'the Peak' that may have made this the kings' choice.
Inside any Ramesside tomb, look up: a dark blue ceiling with yellow stars, or the goddess Nut, means you are under the night sky.
Greek graffiti near the entrances of KV2 and KV9: names left by tourists in Roman times.
fun_fact: In 1912 the American excavator Theodore Davis declared the valley 'exhausted'. Ten years later Howard Carter found Tutankhamun.
narration: Welcome to the Valley of the Kings, the dry gully where Egypt's pharaohs were buried for almost 500 years. Why here, and not under pyramids? Because every pyramid had been robbed. So from about 1539 BC the kings hid their tombs deep in this valley, guarded by police, and built their temples far away by the fields. Thutmose the First's architect, Ineni, boasted that he dug the king's tomb with no one seeing and no one hearing. Look up and you will see a second reason: the peak above you, the Qurn, is shaped like a natural pyramid. There are 65 numbered tombs, but only about 20 held kings. The early ones bend sharply to the side, the later ones run straight into the hill like long pipes, which is exactly what Greek visitors called them. Their walls are guidebooks to the afterlife, and they all tell one story: the sun dies at dusk, sails through the twelve hours of the night, and is reborn at dawn, with the king on board. How to choose? If you buy the extras, take Ramesses the Sixth for the painted sky and Seti the First for the finest carving in Egypt. On the standard ticket, try Ramesses the Fourth, Merenptah, Ramesses the Third or the double tomb of Tausert and Setnakht. Now look at the sign beside the nearest tomb door: it shows the plan, so you know how deep you are about to go.

summary: The smallest royal tomb you will enter held the only nearly intact pharaoh's burial ever found, and Tutankhamun himself still lies here.
look: Sixteen steps and an 8-metre corridor take you down into the antechamber, where Carter's 'wonderful things' were piled; today it holds Tutankhamun's mummy in a glass climate case. To your right, a step down behind a barrier, is the burial chamber, 4 by 6.4 metres, the only decorated room, with the quartzite sarcophagus in the middle. The treasury and annexe beyond are empty.
story:
Howard Carter had searched for years with money from Lord Carnarvon when, on 4 November 1922, his men found a step cut in the rock below the remains of huts used by the builders of Ramesses VI's tomb. A Qurna family tradition gives the find to a water boy, Hussein Abdel Rassoul; Carter's own account credits his workmen. On 26 November Carter made a hole in the sealed door and held up a candle. Asked if he could see anything, he answered, as he later wrote it, 'Yes, wonderful things.'

The tomb is tiny for a king: four rooms, probably a private tomb adapted in a hurry when Tutankhamun died at about 18. Robbers got in twice soon after the burial and it was resealed; later, flood debris and workmen's huts buried the entrance, which saved it. Carnarvon died of an infection in April 1923, and the 'curse' was born.

Only the burial chamber is painted. On the north wall Ay, the next king, in a leopard skin, performs the Opening of the Mouth on the mummy: by burying Tutankhamun he claimed the throne. The east wall shows the funeral sledge, the west wall twelve baboons from the first hour of the Amduat. The quartzite sarcophagus, with a granite lid painted to match, has Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Serqet at its corners; the outer gilded coffin lay in it until 2019, when it went to the Grand Egyptian Museum for restoration. The brown spots on the walls are long-dead microbes that grew when the tomb was sealed with damp plaster; the Getty conservation project, finished in 2019, left them alone.

In 2015 Nicholas Reeves argued that two hidden doors lay behind the plaster, perhaps to Nefertiti's burial. Radar that year seemed to agree; scans in 2016 and 2018 found nothing. A 2026 study says chambers are still possible. Most Egyptologists remain doubtful.
details: North wall, right-hand scene: Ay in a leopard skin and blue crown, touching the mummy's mouth with a ritual adze.
West wall: twelve baboons in a grid, greeting the sun at the first hour of the night.
East wall: the mummy on a sledge under a canopy, hauled by officials with white mourning bands.
The brown spots all over the paintings: dead microbes, already there when Carter opened the tomb.
The glass case in the antechamber: Tutankhamun's face, the one pharaoh still lying in his own tomb in this valley.
fun_fact: The innermost of the three coffins is solid gold and weighs 110.4 kilograms, more than most of the men who lifted it out.
narration: You are standing in the tomb of Tutankhamun, the smallest royal tomb in the valley and the most famous. On 4 November 1922 Howard Carter's workmen found a step cut in the rock, buried under the huts of the men who had built Ramesses the Sixth's tomb above. Local tradition says a water boy found it. Three weeks later Carter held a candle to a hole in the sealed door and, in his own words, saw wonderful things. This room, the antechamber, was crammed with beds, chariots and boxes. Today it holds the king himself, in the glass case: a young man who died at about 18, still lying in his own tomb. The burial chamber, a step down to your right, is the only painted room. On the north wall, Ay, the old courtier who became the next king, wears a leopard skin and touches the mummy's mouth to give back its senses. By burying the king, he was claiming the throne. Opposite, twelve baboons greet the sun at the first hour of night. The stone sarcophagus has a goddess spreading her wings at each corner. In 2015 a British Egyptologist argued that hidden doors lay behind these walls, perhaps to Nefertiti's tomb. Later radar scans found nothing, though the debate is not quite dead. Now look closely at the yellow walls: those brown spots are ancient microbes that grew when the tomb was sealed with damp plaster, and died long ago.

summary: The best ceiling in the valley: Nut swallows the sun and gives birth to it overhead, and Roman-era tourists left nearly a thousand graffiti.
look: One long, straight, gently sloping corridor, about 117 metres, wide enough to feel like a hall, with the Book of Gates on one side and the Book of Caverns on the other. Walk to the very end: the vaulted ceiling of the burial chamber holds the sky goddess Nut twice, stretched end to end. On the floor lie the smashed pieces of the stone sarcophagus.
story:
Ramesses V began this tomb, but he died after a few years and his uncle Ramesses VI took it over, recarving the names and digging deeper. His workmen broke by accident into an older tomb, KV12. More usefully for us, they built their huts on the rubble just below, right on top of a forgotten little tomb: Tutankhamun's, which stayed hidden until 1922.

The decoration is the richest in the valley. The corridors carry the Book of Gates and the Book of Caverns, then eleven hours of the Amduat, then spells from the Book of the Dead in the hall before the burial chamber. The burial chamber walls carry the Books of the Earth. Overhead, the Book of the Day and the Book of the Night are framed by a double figure of Nut: at evening she swallows the sun, it travels through her body by night, and at dawn she gives birth to it again.

Thieves came within decades. A papyrus records the robbery of Ramesses VI's tomb around 1118 BC, and his mummy, hacked about by robbers, was found in 1898 among the kings rewrapped and hidden in Amenhotep II's tomb.

In Greek and Roman times this was 'the tomb of Memnon', named after the Ethiopian hero of the Trojan War, and a must-see. Visitors left 995 graffiti between the 1st century BC and the 4th century AD, mostly in Greek, some in Latin, Demotic and Coptic; Polish epigraphers have studied them since 1996. A doctor named Dadouchios punned on his name, 'torch-bearer'. Another visitor grumbled: 'I did not like anything except the sarcophagus!'
details: Burial chamber ceiling: two figures of Nut back to back, the Book of the Day on one side, the Book of the Night on the other.
Red sun discs travelling along Nut's body: follow one from her mouth to her womb.
Burial chamber walls: the Book of the Earth, with the sun dragged through the underworld by rows of gods.
The pillared hall: winged cobras flank the ramp down to the second corridor.
Near the entrance: Greek graffiti in black and red ink, left by tourists of the Roman era.
fun_fact: One graffito may be signed 'Ambros', which some read as Amr ibn al-As, the Arab general who conquered Egypt in the 7th century. If so, even the conqueror stopped to look at the ceiling.
narration: Welcome to the tomb of Ramesses the Fifth and Ramesses the Sixth. Walk to the end and look up: this is the best ceiling in the valley. Ramesses the Fifth began the tomb and died young. His uncle, Ramesses the Sixth, took it over, recarved the names and pushed the corridor deeper into the hill. As they dug, his workmen built their huts on the rubble outside, right on top of a forgotten little tomb lower down. That tomb was Tutankhamun's, and those huts kept it hidden until 1922. As you walk down, the walls tell the sun's night journey, gate by gate and cavern by cavern. In the burial chamber, the vaulted ceiling shows the sky goddess Nut twice, stretched end to end. Every evening she swallows the sun. Through the night it travels inside her body, and every morning she gives birth to it again. The dead king hoped to ride along. Thieves broke in within a few decades and smashed the sarcophagus, whose pieces still lie on the floor. Then came the tourists. Greeks and Romans called this the tomb of Memnon, after the hero of the Trojan War, and left nearly 1,000 graffiti, mostly in Greek. One visitor wrote that he liked nothing here except the sarcophagus. Now look for the small red sun discs moving along Nut's body overhead, and follow one from her mouth to her womb.

summary: The finest tomb in the valley: 137 metres of carved and painted relief under a starry vault, with a tunnel plunging 174 metres further into the rock.
look: A long descent of stairs and corridors, every wall carved in raised relief and painted, through pillared halls to the vaulted burial chamber, whose ceiling shows constellations in gold on deep blue. The sarcophagus is gone; below where it stood, a tunnel runs down into the rock, closed to visitors. It is steep and warm; give it time.
story:
On 16 October 1817 Giovanni Belzoni, a giant former circus strongman from Padua, broke into this tomb and knew at once he had something extraordinary. It belonged to Seti I, father of Ramesses II, and at 137 metres it was the longest tomb known in the valley until KV5 was explored in the 1990s. Seti was not at home: under King Shoshenq I, in the 10th century BC, priests had moved his mummy to the Deir el-Bahari cache. It is now at NMEC, with one of the best-preserved royal faces of all.

Nothing was skimped. Every wall is carved in raised relief and painted: the Litany of Ra, the Amduat, the Book of Gates, the Opening of the Mouth, and the Book of the Heavenly Cow, in which Ra nearly wipes out humankind. The vaulted burial chamber is one of the first in the valley, its ceiling painted with the constellations. In one side room the work stops at the drawing stage, figures in red and black outline.

Belzoni found a sarcophagus of translucent alabaster carved with the Book of Gates. The British consul Henry Salt sold it to the architect Sir John Soane; it has been in his London house-museum since 1824, and Soane threw a party by lamplight to show it off. The tomb paid for its fame: Belzoni's wax squeezes stripped paint, Champollion cut out a panel 2.26 metres high now in the Louvre, Lepsius took more to Berlin, and floods and later digging cracked the walls.

From beneath the sarcophagus a tunnel slopes into the mountain. A 1960 attempt cleared 136 metres before crumbling rock forced a halt. Zahi Hawass's team finished the job in 2007-10, with steel supports and a little railway: 174 metres, two staircases, then it simply stops. Nobody knows what the builders were aiming for.
details: Burial chamber vault: the constellations and gods of the night sky, in gold on deep blue.
The pillars: Seti face to face with the gods, each figure carved first and painted after.
A side room off the first pillared hall: scenes left as red and black outline drawings, the artists' first draft.
Sharp-edged gaps in some walls: where panels were cut out for the Louvre, Florence and Berlin.
Look closely at any face of Seti: eyelid, ear and lip are modelled in the stone, not just painted.
fun_fact: Belzoni rebuilt two of the tomb's halls at full size for an exhibition at London's Egyptian Hall in 1821: one of the first blockbuster museum replicas.
narration: Most Egyptologists would call this the finest tomb in the valley: the resting place of Seti the First, father of Ramesses the Second. It runs 137 metres into the rock, and nothing was skimped: every figure was carved in raised relief and then painted. It was found on 16 October 1817 by Giovanni Belzoni, a giant former circus strongman from Padua turned explorer. The king was not at home. Priests had moved his mummy to a hiding place near Deir el-Bahari, and today his calm, beautifully preserved face is at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Cairo. Belzoni found only the sarcophagus, carved from translucent alabaster. It was sold to the London architect Sir John Soane, who threw a party by lamplight to show it off, and it is still in his house-museum. The tomb paid for its fame. Wax copies pulled off the paint, Champollion cut out a wall panel that is now in the Louvre, and other pieces went to Florence and Berlin. As you walk down, the walls guide Seti through the hours of the night. In the burial chamber, the vaulted ceiling is a map of the sky, gold stars on deep blue. Below where the sarcophagus stood, a tunnel slopes 174 metres into the mountain, cleared only in 2010, and then it simply stops. Before you leave, look closely at one face of Seti: the eyelid, the ear, the line of the lip, all cut by hand.

summary: Two kings, one wrong turn and a pair of blind harpers: Ramesses III's long tomb has rare scenes of royal kitchens, boats and armouries.
look: A long tomb, 188 metres, entered from the main valley path. Small side rooms open off the first corridors, painted with scenes of royal supplies: bakers, boats, weapons. Further on, the corridor shifts sideways where the first builders hit another tomb, then runs on to an eight-pillared burial chamber.
story:
Setnakht, founder of the 20th Dynasty, started this tomb. His workmen broke straight into the older tomb of Amenmesse, KV10, so he gave up and took over Queen Tausert's tomb, KV14, instead. His son Ramesses III restarted here, shifted the axis sideways to dodge the collision and pushed on to 188 metres.

The side rooms off the first corridors are unlike anything else in the valley: bakers and butchers at work, the king's boats under sail, weapons and armour, the fields of the afterlife. In one, two blind harpers play for the gods. The Scottish traveller James Bruce copied them in 1768, and the tomb has been called 'Bruce's tomb' or the Harpers' Tomb ever since.

The main corridors carry the Litany of Ra, the Amduat and the Book of Gates; the burial chamber has the Book of the Earth. The sarcophagus left in the 19th century: the box is in the Louvre, the lid in the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge.

Ramesses III, who beat the Sea Peoples, died in a palace plot; CT scans in 2012 showed his throat had been cut. His mummy was found in the Deir el-Bahari cache in 1881 and is now at NMEC.
details: Side rooms of the first corridors: bakers, butchers and cooks preparing food for the king's afterlife.
The harpers' room: two blind musicians with tall harps, singing before the gods.
Another side room: bows, quivers, spears and armour lined up like an inventory.
Where the corridor steps sideways: the spot where the first builders broke into KV10 and had to dodge.
The burial chamber: eight pillars and the Book of the Earth on the walls.
fun_fact: James Bruce went on to find the source of the Blue Nile, and London refused to believe half his stories. His harpers, at least, are right here.
narration: You are in the tomb of Ramesses the Third, the last great warrior pharaoh, and it was not his idea. His father, Setnakht, started digging here, but the workmen broke straight into an older royal tomb next door. Setnakht gave up and moved into somebody else's tomb instead. His son restarted, shifted the corridor sideways to dodge the collision, and carried on until it was 188 metres long. Look into the small side rooms near the start. They are unlike anything else in the valley: bakers and butchers at work, the royal boats, racks of weapons and armour. In one of them two blind harpers play for the gods. A Scottish traveller, James Bruce, copied them in 1768, and ever since this has been called the Harpers' Tomb. The king himself had a grim end. He was murdered in a palace plot, and scans in 2012 showed that his throat had been cut. His mummy is now in Cairo, and his sarcophagus is split between the Louvre and Cambridge. Find the harpers, and look at their blank, closed eyes.

summary: A good first tomb: short, bright and easy, and the ancient architect's plan of it survives on a papyrus in Turin.
look: Near the valley entrance, KV2 runs straight and gently downhill for about 89 metres: three corridors, a small hall, then the burial chamber, where the big granite sarcophagus still stands, almost filling the room. The sky goddess Nut stretches across the burial chamber ceiling. Coptic graffiti and painted crosses cluster on the right-hand wall by the entrance.
story:
Ramesses IV, a son of Ramesses III, came to the throne late in life and reigned about six years. He was in a hurry: an ostracon records that the site was chosen in his second year by the local governor and two royal attendants, and the gang of tomb builders at Deir el-Medina was doubled to 120 men.

The tomb is simple, straight and broad. Its walls carry the Litany of Ra, the Book of Caverns, the Amduat and spells from the Book of the Dead, and Nut arches over the sarcophagus. Robbers broke the sarcophagus, probably in antiquity; the king's mummy was rewrapped and hidden in Amenhotep II's tomb, where it was found in 1898.

What makes KV2 special is a document. A papyrus in Turin's Egyptian Museum shows this very tomb in plan, drawn to scale with measurements in hieratic, and the sarcophagus surrounded by four nested shrines: exactly what Carter found around Tutankhamun. Someone also scratched a rough plan on a limestone slab near the entrance, perhaps a workman's doodle.

KV2 has been open since antiquity. Greek and Roman tourists left 656 graffiti, second only to KV9, and Coptic monks seem to have lived here, painting saints and crosses and leaving about 50 inscriptions.
details: Right-hand wall by the entrance: Coptic graffiti, crosses and figures of saints left by monks.
Burial chamber ceiling: the sky goddess Nut stretched over the sarcophagus.
The granite sarcophagus: still in place, damaged by robbers long ago.
First corridor: Greek names scratched by visitors of the Roman era.
fun_fact: The Turin plan shows the shrines around the sarcophagus so precisely that it matches the layout Carter found intact in Tutankhamun's tomb.
narration: Short, bright and easy, the tomb of Ramesses the Fourth makes a good first tomb. Ramesses the Fourth, a son of Ramesses the Third, became king late in life and knew he had little time. In his second year the site was chosen, and the gang of tomb builders was doubled to 120 men. Walk down the gentle slope and notice how simple the plan is: three straight corridors, a small hall and the burial chamber. We know exactly what the builders intended, because the architect's plan survives. It is on a papyrus now in Turin, drawn to scale with measurements in Egyptian script, showing the sarcophagus inside four nested shrines, exactly as Carter later found them around Tutankhamun. This tomb has stood open since antiquity. Greek and Roman tourists left more than 600 graffiti, and later Coptic monks lived here. In the burial chamber, the granite sarcophagus still stands under the arching body of the sky goddess Nut. On your way out, look at the right-hand wall by the entrance for the monks' crosses and Coptic writing.

summary: Rushed to completion after the king died, this bright tomb belongs to the reign when thieves were put on trial for robbing royal graves.
look: Near the valley entrance, just above KV5 and KV55, a gate and a gentle ramp lead into three corridors, 105 metres in all. In the first corridor the king stands before Ra-Horakhty and Osiris. At the end a ramp drops into the burial chamber: Nut across the vaulted ceiling, the king in his boat on the far wall, and a pit in the floor where the vanished sarcophagus stood.
story:
Ramesses IX ruled for nearly two decades while royal power and the economy drained away. His tomb was unfinished when he died and was completed in a hurry: the side rooms of the first corridor were never decorated, the four-pillared hall never finished. The burial chamber was painted fast, yet it glows with unusual yellows, deep blues and blacks: the Book of Caverns and the Book of the Earth on the walls, Nut overhead.

His reign is famous for crime. The mayor of Thebes, Paser, accused his rival on the west bank, Pawero, of failing to protect the royal tombs. The inquiry survives in the Abbott Papyrus, and the Amherst-Leopold Papyrus preserves the confession of a stonemason, Amenpanufer, who described breaking into the tomb of King Sobekemsaf, stripping the gold and setting fire to the coffins. Another papyrus records eight workmen arrested in year 17 for robbing the tomb of a queen, Isis.

In the end the thieves won. This tomb has stood open since antiquity, with Roman and Coptic graffiti, and the king's mummy was found in the Deir el-Bahari cache in 1881. It is now at NMEC.
details: First corridor: the king offering to the falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty and to Osiris.
Undecorated side rooms in the first corridor: the first sign of the rush after the king's death.
Burial chamber ceiling: Nut twice, back to back, in yellow on dark blue.
Far wall of the burial chamber: Ramesses in his sun boat, surrounded by gods.
The empty pit in the floor: the sarcophagus has vanished.
fun_fact: The great tomb-robbery trials began as a feud between two mayors, one on each bank of the river.
narration: Ramesses the Ninth, whose tomb this is, reigned for nearly two decades while Egypt slowly ran out of money and order. The tomb was not ready when he died, and the workmen finished it in a hurry. You can see the corners they cut: undecorated side rooms near the entrance and a pillared hall never completed. Yet the burial chamber is a delight, painted fast in strong yellow, deep blue and black. His reign is famous for a crime wave. The mayor of Thebes accused his rival, the mayor of the west bank, of letting thieves plunder the royal tombs, and the inquiry still survives on papyrus. One stonemason confessed to breaking into an old king's tomb, stripping the gold from the mummies and setting fire to the coffins. Eight workmen were arrested for robbing a queen's tomb. In the end the thieves won here too. This tomb has stood open since antiquity, and the king's mummy was found in 1881 in the priests' hiding place near Deir el-Bahari. In the burial chamber, look up at the sky goddess Nut stretched across the vaulted ceiling.

summary: Ramesses II's 13th son finally became king, and his nested stone sarcophagi were so big the builders had to tear out the doorframes.
look: A long, steep descent: the burial chamber lies at the end of 160 metres of corridor. Near the entrance the reliefs are deep and fine; lower down, ancient floodwater has damaged the walls. Deep inside lies a huge granite sarcophagus lid with Merenptah carved as Osiris.
story:
Ramesses II reigned 66 years and outlived a dozen crown princes. His 13th son, Merenptah, finally took the throne as an old man and ruled about ten years. He is best known for his victory stela, which contains the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible.

His tomb was built for four stone sarcophagi, one inside another. The outer one was so large that the builders demolished the doorjambs to get it in, then rebuilt them with inscribed sandstone blocks held by dovetail cramps; they also cut away pillars in the hall. Two of those pillars may have been stolen by Paneb, a notorious Deir el-Medina workman whose crimes were recorded in court.

About two centuries later, in the Third Intermediate Period, the outer sarcophagus was smashed to get at an inner one, which King Psusennes I reused for his own burial at Tanis in the Delta. Merenptah's mummy had been moved to the cache in Amenhotep II's tomb, where Victor Loret found it in 1898.

The walls carry the Amduat and the Book of Gates. Open since antiquity and low in the valley, the tomb has suffered from floods.
details: Start of the first corridor: Merenptah greeting the falcon-headed sun god Ra-Horakhty.
The doorways along the corridor: look for fitted sandstone blocks where the original jambs were knocked out.
The granite lid: Merenptah as Osiris, arms crossed, protected by the gods.
Lower walls: bare, scoured stone where floods stripped the plaster.
fun_fact: Merenptah outlived twelve older brothers to become king; two centuries after his death, another pharaoh borrowed his sarcophagus.
narration: Merenptah, whose tomb you are entering, was the 13th son of Ramesses the Second. His father reigned 66 years and outlived twelve of his older sons, so Merenptah came to the throne as an old man and ruled about ten years. He is famous for a victory stela that mentions Israel for the first time outside the Bible. The corridor runs steeply down for 160 metres, and it had a problem. Merenptah ordered four stone sarcophagi, one inside another, and the outer one was too big to fit. So the builders knocked out the door frames, moved it through, and rebuilt them with sandstone blocks. They also cut away pillars in the hall, and some Egyptologists suspect a notorious workman called Paneb carried off two of them. About two centuries later, priests smashed the outer sarcophagus to get at an inner one, and King Psusennes reused it for his own burial in the Delta. Merenptah's mummy was hidden elsewhere and is now in Cairo. As you go down, look for the great granite lid with the king carved as Osiris, arms crossed, ready for eternity.

period: New Kingdom, late 19th to early 20th Dynasty, c. 1191-1186 BC
summary: A queen who ruled as pharaoh began this tomb; the man who replaced her painted himself over her figures and moved in.
look: One of the largest tombs in the valley, over 112 metres, in the southern part of the valley next to KV15. It runs straight through corridors and two burial chambers, one after the other: first Tausert's, then Setnakht's extension. Look on the walls and pillars for figures redone in ink where a queen once stood.
story:
Tausert was the great royal wife of Seti II. When he died the throne went to a sickly boy, Siptah, with Tausert and the chancellor Bay as the real power. Bay was executed in Siptah's fifth year, Siptah died young, and Tausert ruled alone as king, one of very few women to do so, after Sobekneferu and Hatshepsut.

Her tomb grew with her: begun for a queen, enlarged with a royal burial chamber when she became king. Seti II may even have been buried here first and moved later to the hastily finished KV15 next door.

Then Setnakht, founder of the 20th Dynasty, took over. We do not know how Tausert's reign ended, but he moved into her tomb. Her images were erased and replaced with his, and he cut further into the hill to add a second burial chamber, making this one of the largest royal tombs.

So you walk through two reigns stitched together. Tausert's mummy has never been securely identified: among the bodies hidden in Amenhotep II's tomb was an unknown woman lying in an upturned coffin lid inscribed for Setnakht, and some think she may be Tausert. The tomb was properly recorded only when Hartwig Altenmuller excavated it in 1983-87.
details: Pillars and walls: places where a woman's figure was erased and Setnakht painted over her in simple ink.
The first burial chamber with its pillars: Tausert's royal chamber.
The corridor continuing beyond it: Setnakht's extension to his own second burial chamber.
Scenes of Anubis, Isis and the four sons of Horus guarding the dead.
fun_fact: A tomb with two owners may have had three: Tausert's husband Seti II was perhaps buried here first and moved out.
narration: You are in a tomb with two owners, and you can still see the takeover. It was begun for Tausert, the wife of Seti the Second. After her husband died, a sickly boy, Siptah, became king, with Tausert and a powerful chancellor called Bay pulling the strings. Bay was executed, the boy died young, and Tausert ruled Egypt as king in her own right, one of very few women ever to do so. Her tomb grew with her ambitions into one of the largest in the valley. Then her reign ended, we do not know how, and a new king, Setnakht, founder of the next dynasty, moved in. He had her figures erased and painted himself on top, then dug on and added a second burial chamber beyond hers. Her own mummy has never been securely identified. So as you walk down, you are walking through two reigns stitched together. Look at the pillars for figures redone in simple ink: in at least one, the queen was erased and Setnakht painted where she had stood.

summary: A tomb that ran out of time: fine relief at the door, then paint, then hasty sketches, as Seti II's short reign ended.
look: At the head of a side wadi, at the foot of a sheer cliff beside KV14. Short corridors lead to a well room where the well was never dug, a pillared hall, and a corridor turned into a burial chamber. Only the sarcophagus lid remains.
story: Seti II reigned less than six years and lost Thebes for part of that time to a rival, Amenmesse. You can watch the clock run out: carved relief near the entrance, then painted plaster, then quick sketches. Seti's name was carved, erased, probably by Amenmesse's people, and carved again. The well room has unusual paintings of the king's funerary statues, standing on a panther or in a papyrus skiff, just like the gilded figures later found with Tutankhamun. Seti may first have been buried in KV14, then moved here; his mummy turned up in the cache in Amenhotep II's tomb. From 1922 Carter's colleagues Alfred Lucas and Arthur Mace used this tomb as their laboratory, cleaning and conserving Tutankhamun's treasures before they went to Cairo.
details: Near the entrance: crisp carved relief. Walk on and watch it give way to paint, then sketches.
Well room walls: the king's funerary statuettes, one standing on a panther's back.
The lid of Seti's sarcophagus, the only piece of his burial still in the tomb.
fun_fact: Tutankhamun's gilded statuette of a king on a panther was cleaned in this tomb, a few metres from a 3,200-year-old painting of the same kind of statue.
narration: Here is a tomb that ran out of time: the tomb of Seti the Second. Seti reigned less than six years. Walk in and watch the work get faster. Near the door the figures are carved in fine relief. Further in they are only painted, and in places only sketched. In the well room, where a shaft was planned but never dug, the painters showed the king's funeral statues, one standing on the back of a panther. Exactly that kind of gilded statue was later found in Tutankhamun's tomb, and in the 1920s Carter's team used this very tomb as their laboratory to clean his treasures. Look at the relief by the entrance, then compare it with the quick brushwork inside.

summary: An old general's tiny tomb, painted in a rush and glowing with colour; his mummy spent over 130 years as a curiosity at Niagara Falls.
look: Only 29 metres long: two steep staircases and a sloping corridor lead straight down to a single burial chamber. The red granite sarcophagus, painted rather than carved, still stands in the middle. Around it the king meets the gods in bright colours on a blue-grey background, with scenes from the Book of Gates.
story:
Ramesses I was born Paramessu, into a military family from the Nile Delta. He rose to be vizier to Horemheb, the last king of the 18th Dynasty, who had no surviving children and chose him as heir. He reigned less than two years, but he founded a dynasty: his son was Seti I and his grandson Ramesses II.

The tomb shows the haste. There was only time for one room; the walls got a quick coat of plaster and paint, and the sarcophagus was painted instead of carved, with a number of mistakes in its texts. The result is one of the brightest rooms in the valley, close in style to Horemheb's tomb. Belzoni found it on 10 October 1817, six days before Seti I's.

His mummy had an odyssey. Taken from the Deir el-Bahari cache by the Abd el-Rassul family, it was sold to a Canadian doctor, James Douglas, and around 1860 ended up in the Niagara Falls Museum, displayed for more than 130 years. In 1999 the Michael C. Carlos Museum in Atlanta bought it, and on 24 October 2003 it returned to Egypt. It is now in the Luxor Museum, which you visit on the 22nd.
details: The walls: figures on a blue-grey background, painted straight onto plaster in a hurry.
The king led by the gods: look for falcon-headed Horus and jackal-headed Anubis beside him.
The red granite sarcophagus: its figures and texts painted, not carved.
Book of Gates: the sun's boat towed through the night, in rows of small figures.
fun_fact: For over a century the founder of the Ramesside dynasty shared a museum at Niagara Falls with stuffed animals and the barrels of daredevils who had gone over the falls.
narration: This small, brilliant room is the tomb of Ramesses the First, founder of the dynasty of Seti and Ramesses the Great. He began life as Paramessu, an army officer from the Delta, and rose to be vizier for King Horemheb, who had no sons and named him heir. He reigned less than two years. So his tomb is tiny, just 29 metres, one room at the bottom of two staircases. The painters had to work fast, straight onto plaster, and the result is one of the brightest rooms in the valley, figures glowing against a blue-grey sky. Even the red granite sarcophagus is painted rather than carved, with a few spelling mistakes. His mummy had a stranger journey than the man. Stolen by tomb robbers in the 19th century, it was sold to a collector and spent more than 130 years in a museum at Niagara Falls. In 2003 it came home, and it now lies in the Luxor Museum, which you will visit tomorrow. Look at the wall where the king is led by the gods, and notice the confident, unhesitating lines.
